questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are non-tender and rubbery. VDRL is non-reactive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) presents as a single, painless, indurated ulcer with non-tender rubbery lymphadenopathy. VDRL may be non-reactive in early primary syphilis (serological window period). Diagnosis is confirmed by dark-field microscopy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops a malar rash after sun exposure. Skin biopsy shows immunoglobulin and complement deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. This finding is called:
questions.exp: The lupus band test (direct immunofluorescence) demonstrates deposition of IgG, IgM, IgA, and complement (C3) at the dermoepidermal junction in both lesional and non-lesional skin of SLE patients, distinguishing it from discoid lupus where only lesional skin is positive.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with multiple verrucous plaques on the foot and lower leg. KOH mount shows 'copper penny' or 'medlar bodies' (sclerotic cells). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused most commonly by Fonsecaea pedrosoi. It presents as verrucous plaques and the hallmark on histology is 'muriform cells' (medlar bodies/copper penny cells) — thick-walled, brown, septate cells that reproduce by equatorial splitting.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with multiple sexual partners presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the prepuce, associated with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Herpes genitalis (HSV-2 usually) presents with grouped vesicles and multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear. Treatment is oral acyclovir 200 mg 5 times/day for 7-10 days for first episode. Valacyclovir and famciclovir are alternatives.

questions.q: A 30-year-old leprosy patient on dapsone monotherapy develops acute haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. The most likely cause is:
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-related haemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency) and methaemoglobinaemia in all patients to some degree. Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS) presents with rash, fever, and internal organ involvement, typically in the first 6 weeks, and is idiosyncratic.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with tense blisters on normal and erythematous skin. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The autoantigen targeted is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense blisters, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. The autoantigens are BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1). BP180 is the major pathogenic antigen.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male smoker presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose that has grown slowly over 2 years. The most appropriate treatment with lowest recurrence rate is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) — the most common skin malignancy. Mohs micrographic surgery has the lowest recurrence rate (1-2% for primary BCC) as it allows complete margin assessment. It is treatment of choice for high-risk locations (face, especially H-zone), large tumours, and recurrent lesions.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed areas, and hypertrichosis. Urine turns pink on exposure to sunlight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) presents with photosensitivity, skin fragility, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Urine fluoresces pink-red under Wood's lamp due to excess uroporphyrins. It is the most common porphyria and is associated with HCV, alcohol, and iron overload.

questions.q: A leprosy patient classified as PB (2 patches) presents with acute swelling and redness of existing patches with new patches and nerve pain. There is no systemic illness. The most likely reaction is:
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction seen in BT, BB, BL patients. It presents with erythema and oedema of existing patches, new lesions, and acute neuritis. Type 2 (ENL) occurs in BL and LL patients and features tender erythematous nodules with systemic features.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents with well-defined hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation and absence of sweating. Slit-skin smear is negative. Nerve biopsy shows granulomas with Langhans giant cells. What is the classification?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows high cell-mediated immunity: single/few well-defined hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, absent sweating, slit-skin smear negative (paucibacillary), and granulomas with Langhans cells on biopsy. LL is at the opposite pole with diffuse infiltration and high bacterial load.

questions.q: A 29-year-old male presents with painful genital ulcers that are soft, non-indurated, with undermined edges and a necrotic base. Inguinal nodes are tender and fluctuant (buboes). Gram stain shows 'school of fish' pattern. Treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful soft ulcer and tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes). Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish/railroad track' pattern. Azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose are recommended.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male presents with silvery-white scaly plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp. Removal of scales reveals pinpoint bleeding. This sign is known as:
questions.exp: Auspitz sign is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding on removal of psoriatic scales. It results from the elongated dermal papillae with thin suprapapillary epidermis, so removal of scales exposes these vessels. It is characteristic of psoriasis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for SLE develops blurring of vision. The most likely ocular toxicity is:
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine causes bull's eye maculopathy (parafoveal damage) on long-term use. Recommended screening includes baseline and annual ophthalmological examination. Corneal deposits (reversible) can also occur but are less clinically significant. Maximum safe dose is ≤5 mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with grouped vesiculopustules around the nose and mouth that rupture leaving honey-coloured crusts. Culture grows beta-haemolytic Streptococcus. The most serious complication to watch for is:
questions.exp: Impetigo caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A Streptococcus (GAS) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Unlike pharyngeal GAS infection, skin impetigo does NOT cause rheumatic fever. PSGN presents 2-3 weeks after skin infection with haematuria and hypertension.

questions.q: A 42-year-old diabetic male presents with a rapidly spreading, tender, erythematous area on the leg with crepitus on palpation. X-ray shows gas in soft tissues. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Urgent surgical debridement with IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis (Type 1 polymicrobial in diabetics) is a surgical emergency. Gas in soft tissues (crepitus) is a hallmark. Immediate wide surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics is the treatment. Delay significantly increases mortality.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with scaly erythematous plaques in a butterfly distribution over the cheeks and nose, sparing the nasolabial folds. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: The malar (butterfly) rash of SLE characteristically involves the cheeks and bridge of nose but spares the nasolabial folds. Rosacea involves the nasolabial folds and has telangiectasias/pustules. Seborrhoeic dermatitis involves nasolabial folds and scalp. DLE causes scarring disc-shaped lesions.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with annular, scaly plaques with central clearing on the trunk. KOH mount shows hyphae. The most effective topical agent is:
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (dermatophytosis) responds best to topical terbinafine (allylamine) which is fungicidal. Nystatin is only for Candida. Griseofulvin and amphotericin B are not routinely used topically for tinea. Topical azoles are also effective but terbinafine has faster cure rates.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male with a history of actinic keratoses presents with a rapidly growing nodule on the lower lip with a central keratin-filled crater that has been present for 6 weeks. This is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is characterized by rapid growth (weeks) of a crateriform nodule with central keratin plug, followed by spontaneous involution. It clinically resembles SCC (and some consider it a low-grade SCC variant). Sun-exposed areas in older men are typical. Often managed by excision.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting on the abdomen, sparing the periumbilical area. This condition is:
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) typically occurs in primigravidas in the third trimester. It starts in striae on the abdomen and characteristically spares the periumbilical area. It is benign and resolves postpartum. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically and forms tense blisters.

questions.q: A child presents with multiple flesh-coloured dome-shaped papules with central umbilication on the trunk and genitals. The causative virus belongs to which family?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxviridae family. It presents as dome-shaped papules with central umbilication containing caseous material (molluscum bodies/Henderson-Paterson bodies on histology).

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with nodular, hyperpigmented lesions on the lower extremities associated with lower limb lymphoedema. He is from a coastal endemic area. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma (endemic type in Africa/Asia) presents with violaceous/hyperpigmented nodules on lower extremities with lymphoedema. KS is caused by HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus). In India, it can be seen in endemic coastal regions. Biopsy shows spindle cells lining slit-like vascular spaces.

questions.q: A patient with recurrent aphthous stomatitis is found to have low serum ferritin and folate levels. Replacement of these deficiencies is likely to benefit patients with which type of aphthous ulcer?
questions.exp: Haematinic deficiencies (iron, folate, B12) are associated with recurrent aphthous stomatitis, particularly the herpetiform type. Replacement therapy can reduce frequency and severity in deficient patients. RAS is also associated with coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.q: A 23-year-old female presents with painful vasospastic episodes involving fingers that turn white, then blue, then red on cold exposure. She has puffy fingers and sclerodactyly. ANA is positive with anti-Scl-70 antibody. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and positive ANA. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is specific for diffuse cutaneous SSc and is associated with pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc (CREST syndrome).

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with itchy, purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules on the flexor surface of the wrists. White lacy pattern is visible on the buccal mucosa. The pathological process is:
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated (Type IV/delayed) hypersensitivity condition with CD8+ T cells targeting basal keratinocytes expressing altered self-antigens. Classic features: pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules (5 P's) with Wickham's striae on mucosa.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male (CD4 count 80/mm³) presents with violaceous patches and plaques on the hard palate and lower extremities. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Local radiation therapy for oral lesion and HAART
questions.exp: AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma: HAART is the cornerstone of treatment and can lead to regression of KS lesions by immune reconstitution. Localized lesions may need local therapy (radiation, intralesional vinblastine). Systemic chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin) is reserved for extensive/visceral disease.

questions.q: An 18-year-old female presents with streaky linear vesicles in a dermatomal distribution on the trunk following a recent chickenpox episode. The immediate treatment is:
opts: Oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunocompetent patient: oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days is standard. Famciclovir 500 mg TDS or valacyclovir 1 g TDS are equally effective and preferred for compliance. IV acyclovir is reserved for immunocompromised patients, disseminated zoster, or ophthalmic involvement.

questions.q: A 34-year-old female with diffuse hair loss undergoing work-up has positive pull test, predominantly telogen hairs on trichogram, and a history of major surgery 3 months ago. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium occurs 2-4 months after a triggering event (surgery, fever, childbirth, crash diet). There is diffuse hair shedding with predominantly telogen hairs on trichogram. It is generally reversible. Anagen effluvium occurs within days-weeks (e.g., after chemotherapy) with predominantly anagen hair loss.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on the lower legs, arthralgia, and haematuria. Serum C3 and C4 are low. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits. The most likely underlying diagnosis is:
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (HSP) presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and nephritis. IgA deposits in skin and kidney are diagnostic. It is the most common vasculitis in children but also occurs in adults. Low complement is more typical of cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis; in HSP complement is usually normal.

questions.q: A patient undergoes patch testing for contact dermatitis. The patch is applied for 48 hours. Reading is done at 48 hours and 96 hours. A reaction showing erythema, oedema, and vesicles at 96 hours (but not at 48 hours) is most consistent with:
opts: Allergic contact dermatitis — late positive reaction
questions.exp: Patch testing detects Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity causing allergic contact dermatitis. Late positives appearing at 96 hours (D4) are common with certain allergens like metals (especially gold), neomycin, and corticosteroids. Reading at 48h and 96h is standard to detect both early and late reactions.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with hypopigmented macules on the upper trunk with fine scales on scratching (Besnier's sign). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatball' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (Malassezia globosa). KOH mount shows characteristic thick-walled yeast cells and short curved hyphae — 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green or coppery-orange fluorescence. Treatment: topical selenium sulphide, azoles, or oral itraconazole.
